title: Fermat Tests and Pseudoprimes
short: If aⁿ⁻¹ ≢ 1 (mod n) for some a with 1 < a < n, then n is composite; passing the test does not prove that n is prime.
trouble: Students treat the converse of Fermat's theorem as true, but 2³⁴⁰ ≡ 1 (mod 341) and 341 = 11 · 31.

blocks.html: Fermat's theorem gives a fast way to show a number is composite without finding a factor. That is how computers screen the huge numbers used in cryptography. But the test has a blind spot, and knowing exactly what it proves is the lesson here.
The Fermat test. To test $n$, pick a base $a$ with $1 < a < n - 1$ and compute $a^{n-1} \bmod n$ by repeated squaring.

items: If $a^{n-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$, then $n$ passes: it is probably prime, but not proven prime.

blocks.html: Fermat's theorem says: if $n$ is prime (and $n \nmid a$), then $a^{n-1} \equiv 1$. Its contrapositive is just as true: if $a^{n-1} \not\equiv 1$, then $n$ is not prime. But the converse, "if $a^{n-1} \equiv 1$ then $n$ is prime," is a different statement, and it is false. A composite $n$ with $a^{n-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$ is called a pseudoprime to base $a$.

blocks.title: Caught by the test
steps: $2^{90} \equiv 64 \not\equiv 1$, so $91$ is composite. (Indeed $91 = 7 \cdot 13$, but the test never needed that.)

blocks.title: A pseudoprime
blocks.q: Show that $341 = 11 \cdot 31$ passes the base-2 test.
steps: $341$ passes, yet it is composite: it is the smallest pseudoprime to base 2.

blocks.html: Changing the base often exposes a pseudoprime: $3^{340} \bmod 341 = 56$, so base 3 catches 341. But $91$ fools base 3 ($3^{6} = 729 = 8 \cdot 91 + 1$, so $3^{90} \equiv 1$), and some composites fool every base coprime to them. These are the Carmichael numbers.

blocks.title: A Carmichael number
blocks.q: Korselt's criterion: a composite $n$ is a Carmichael number exactly when it is squarefree and $p - 1 \mid n - 1$ for every prime $p \mid n$. Check $561 = 3 \cdot 11 \cdot 17$.
steps: So $561$ passes the Fermat test for every base coprime to it, though it is composite.
blocks.a: Yes, $561$ is a Carmichael number (the smallest).

blocks.html: Treating the converse of Fermat's theorem as true: "$2^{340} \equiv 1 \pmod{341}$, so 341 is prime." But $341 = 11 \cdot 31$. A result of 1 only means "not caught yet." A result other than 1 is a proof of compositeness. Real primality tests (like Miller–Rabin, a strengthened Fermat test) use several bases and a sharper condition.
If $a^{n-1} \not\equiv 1 \pmod{n}$, then $n$ is composite. If $a^{n-1} \equiv 1$, $n$ may still be composite: a pseudoprime, or for every base at once, a Carmichael number.
